title: A Pipeline Seven Times the River
topics:

---

Cheyenne Light's record peak load is 439 MW. Its near-term data center pipeline is 3 GW, plus another 2.5 GW of "emerging opportunities." Divide it out and the pipeline is nearly seven times the busiest day the system has ever had, or about twelve times if you count the emerging part. Microsoft deals are in the headline, so some of it is real. I just can't tell how much of the 3 GW they cover.

Yesterday Vistra's CEO admitted the queues were padded. Today's earnings roundup says the same thing more politely. Executives who spent the summer reading out pipeline numbers are now stressing "the diversity of sources driving load growth." It's a lovely phrase. It doesn't claim data centers shrank, only that other things are also happening. When a company changes which noun it leads with, the old noun usually had a bad quarter. Affordability and "good relations with incoming officials" show up in nearly every summary too, which is the midterms speaking through an investor-relations department.

My favorite detail is TVA. It just received the first NRC construction permit for a BWRX-300 small modular reactor at Clinch River, and it has "not yet decided" whether to build it. Years of paperwork, and the result sits there like a reservation at a restaurant you may not go to. That's not a criticism. An option is worth something precisely because you don't have to exercise it.

A queue spot works the same way, and that was the problem. It costs almost nothing to hold, so people hold a lot of them. TVA's $1.7B data center deal under its new large-load tariff is the other kind of paper, the kind with a penalty attached. I'd like to know how much of Cheyenne's 3 GW looks like that.
